doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Growing up in Joplin, move to Detroit, musical mother
summary: Born in Joplin, saw territorial bands in the park, moved to Detroit in 1948; an only child whose mother is musical.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Right. Growing up — in Missouri, correct? Did the music that you heard during your childhood have an effect on your eventual choice to be a jazz musician?

Oh I’m sure it did, since everything is connected. I grew up in Joplin, Missouri, which is a little small town south of St. Louis, it’s in the southwest corner of Missouri. It borders Oklahoma and Arkansas. And I was there up until about nine years of age then I moved to Detroit. But during the time that I was there, I did have occasion to see various bands, probably coming from Kansas City. They were probably territorial bands. And you know I was a kid so this is when I was like maybe five, six, seven, eight. And every year in the summertime these bands would come to this park in Joplin and play for like a week. And I was quite impressed with the bands, with the music and with the way the horns look, you know, just the physicalities of the nice, gold, shiny horn. And I did like the music, but I didn’t start playing until I was about 13, in Detroit. And I moved from Joplin, Missouri to Detroit in 1948, I was about nine. And then in junior high school, like intermediate school, I started playing music.
Did you come from a big family?

No, I’m an only child. My mother is quite musical, and I think when she was a kid she played piano. But I didn’t hear it, I didn’t have that around me as a kid. My father, I don’t think he was as musical as my mom, but he did dabble a little bit, but nothing serious. So

I would imagine that I might have gotten whatever I’ve gotten from my mom, I would say so. She’s a natural — how do you say — well she loves music and she truly feels music. It really does something for her. I can tell by the way she listens. And I think, whatever I got is probably from her.
